back: Rerun: same code, same data, same machine, same number. Reproduction: their code and data, my machine. Replication: my own implementation of their method. Each answers a different question.

front: What makes a claim good to reproduce?
back: Specific (setting, arms, metric, direction), falsifiable at your scale, measurable exactly, and interesting if false.

front: What do you do with a setup detail the paper omits?
back: Look in the code release, appendix and related work; otherwise pick a default and log it as a deviation.

front: How many runs does a reproduction plan need?
back: configurations x seeds; check runs x minutes per run against the compute budget before starting.

front: The three verdicts when comparing with a reported number r
back: Reproduced: r is inside the 95 percent interval of my runs. Within tolerance: outside the interval but |mean - r| <= a tolerance fixed in advance. Not reproduced: neither.

front: 95 percent interval of a mean from n runs
back: mean +- t_{n-1,0.975} * s / sqrt(n), with s the sample sd (ddof=1).

front: Interval of the mean vs spread of single runs
back: The interval shrinks like 1/sqrt(n); the spread of single runs stays about s. Check a single reported run against mean +- 2s, not the narrow interval of the mean.

front: Why compare A and B with common random numbers?
back: Same seeds in both arms cancel shared noise (initialisation, batch order); the paired difference d_i = a_i - b_i has a much smaller spread.

front: Order in which to investigate a failed reproduction
back: Unreported details, evaluation differences, leakage, seeds/variance, non-determinism, scale, then the possibility that the claim was weaker than the summary.

front: Why can the same seeded code give different numbers on different hardware?
back: Floating-point summation order, non-deterministic kernels, precision defaults and library versions are not controlled by the seed.

front: A reproduction is much better than the paper. First suspicion?
back: Leakage or a different evaluation (e.g. normalising with full-data statistics, selecting on the test set).

front: What must a reproduction report contain?
back: Claim, source, data, model, hyper-parameters, metric, seeds, environment, deviations (or the word 'none'), results with intervals, a verdict, limits, artifacts (commit, command).

front: In the dropout example, setting 1 vs setting 2?
back: Fixed dataset: gap reduction 0.055, interval [0.045, 0.066]. Resampled datasets: 0.008, interval [-0.010, 0.027]. Wider variance sources can change the verdict.

front: Why must you reproduce the baseline first?
back: It calibrates data, metric, split and training loop; if the baseline's published number is not matched, comparisons with the new method are untrustworthy.

front: Why report the interval with a 'reproduced' verdict?
back: With very few runs the interval is so wide that almost any reported value falls inside; the width shows how much the verdict actually rules out.
